title: Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP)
summary: Replaces RFC 977 as the official specification of the Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP), which carries Usenet-style news articles between servers and readers. It clarifies vagueness in the old specification and incorporates widely used extensions.

plainLanguage.summary: NNTP lets a client read and post news articles and lets servers transfer articles to one another. The client sends commands, the server replies with status codes, and a capability list shows which optional features are available.

subtitle: A command-and-response protocol for reading, posting, and transferring news articles.

tldr.problem: News readers and servers need a standard way to select newsgroups, retrieve or post articles, and transfer articles between servers.
tldr.mechanism: NNTP exchanges commands and numeric responses over a reliable stream; capabilities let a client discover which optional commands and extensions a server supports.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3977 replaces RFC 977, clarifies earlier rules, makes more commands mandatory, and adds capability discovery and a registered-extension mechanism.

today: RFC 3977 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 977 and updates RFC 2980. It is later updated by RFC 6048.

sections.title: The NNTP Service
sections.content:
The Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP) distributes, retrieves, and posts Netnews articles over a reliable, full-duplex stream. A reading client can select articles from a server's store, while servers can transfer articles between their stores.

RFC 3977 replaces RFC 977. It clarifies the protocol, changes the default character set to UTF-8, makes some previously optional commands mandatory, and adds the CAPABILITIES command.
sections.plainLanguage: NNTP is a way for news software to exchange articles with a server. The same protocol supports readers who fetch articles and servers that relay articles to other servers.

sections.title: Commands, Responses, and Article Data
sections.content:
The server sends a greeting after a connection is established. The client then sends one command per line, and the server answers with a three-digit response code. A response may include a multi-line data block, terminated by a line containing a single dot.

Lines in a multi-line block that begin with a dot are sent with an extra dot at the start; the receiver removes that extra dot. Article data consists of headers, a blank line, and a body, and each article has a unique message-id.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends commands and reads numeric replies. Multi-line article data uses a dot line to mark the end, and leading dots are doubled so they cannot be mistaken for that marker.

sections.title: Discovering Capabilities and Extensions
sections.content:
The CAPABILITIES command returns a list describing the server's current features. VERSION is required and must appear first; other labels can indicate reading commands, posting, transfer, and extensions.

A server must accurately reflect its current state in the list. Registered extensions define their capability labels and command behavior; private extension labels begin with X.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can ask which NNTP features a server currently offers. It can use that list to avoid relying on commands the server does not support.

sections.title: Selecting, Retrieving, and Posting Articles
sections.content:
A reading client selects a newsgroup with GROUP, then can move between articles with LAST and NEXT. ARTICLE retrieves the headers and body, while HEAD and BODY retrieve only one part; STAT checks whether an article exists without returning its text.

POST lets a reading client submit a new article after the server grants permission. IHAVE lets a peer server offer an already-posted article for transfer. Both send the article as a multi-line block and receive a final success or failure response.
sections.plainLanguage: GROUP selects a newsgroup, and article commands retrieve all or part of an article. POST submits a new article; IHAVE offers an article from another server.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
NNTP commands can expose personal information, and server logs can reveal client activity. Weak authentication and access controls can allow unauthorized use; DNS spoofing can misdirect clients if names are resolved or cached incorrectly.

Clients and servers that cache host lookups must honor DNS time-to-live information. Capability lists related to security and privacy must not be cached, because the available protections can change with connection state.
sections.plainLanguage: NNTP can expose article activity and account information. Clients should respect DNS cache lifetimes and recheck security-related capabilities for each relevant connection state.
